claim: Approximately 3.7% of genetic variants associated with diseases occur in UTRs.
source: According to the NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog, genome-wide association studies up to 2018 had uncovered that ~3.7% of disease risk/quantitative trait-associated genetic variants are located in UTRs (MacArthur et al., 2017; Steri et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published GWAS catalog data from MacArthur et al., 2017 and Steri et al., 2018.

claim: The average length of the 5' UTR in humans is approximately 210 nucleotides.
source: The average length of the 5' and 3' UTRs in human is ~210 nucleotides (nt) and ~1030 nt, respectively, with mean 3' UTR length being more diverse among species and higher eukaryotes hosting longer 3' UTRs (Pesole et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pesole et al., 2001.

claim: The average length of the 3' UTR in humans is approximately 1030 nucleotides.
source: The average length of the 5' and 3' UTRs in human is ~210 nucleotides (nt) and ~1030 nt, respectively, with mean 3' UTR length being more diverse among species and higher eukaryotes hosting longer 3' UTRs (Pesole et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pesole et al., 2001.

claim: Higher eukaryotes host longer 3' UTRs.
source: The average length of the 5' and 3' UTRs in human is ~210 nucleotides (nt) and ~1030 nt, respectively, with mean 3' UTR length being more diverse among species and higher eukaryotes hosting longer 3' UTRs (Pesole et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pesole et al., 2001.

claim: UTRs contain cis-regulatory elements that contribute to post-transcriptional regulation of gene expression.
source: The UTRs contain cis-regulatory elements that contribute to post-transcriptionally regulating gene expression, such as via protein translation control, subcellular mRNA localization, and mRNA stability upon interactions with trans-acting factors such as RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) and microRNAs (miRNAs) (Barrett et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Barrett et al., 2012.

claim: The miRNA-Argonaute complex recruits the CCR4-NOT complex to initiate deadenylation and decay.
source: For instance, the miRNA-Argonaute complex recruits the CCR4-NOT (Carbon Catabolite Repression—Negative On TATA-less) complex to initiate deadenylation and decay (Huntzinger and Izaurralde, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Huntzinger and Izaurralde, 2011.

claim: AU-rich elements (AREs) in 3' UTRs provide binding sites for ARE-binding proteins that trigger the RNA degradation pathway.
source: Another example is AU-rich elements (AREs, sequence elements rich in adenosine and uridine) present in the 3' UTRs of many mRNAs that provide binding sites for ARE-binding proteins that trigger the RNA degradation pathway (Garneau et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Garneau et al., 2007.

claim: TTP, BRF1, hnRNP D (AUF1), and KSRP are ARE-binding proteins that destabilize mRNA.
source: Many ARE-binding proteins have been characterized to date that are involved in stability regulation of ARE-hosting mRNAs (Barreau et al., 2005), including Tristetrapolin (TTP), Butyrate Response Factor 1 (BRF1), Heterogeneous Nuclear Ribonucleoprotein (hnRNP) D (also known as AU-Rich Element-Binding Protein 1, AUF1), and KH-type splicing regulatory protein (KSRP), all of which destabilize mRNA, unlike ELAV Like RNA Binding Protein 1 (ELAVL1, also known as HuR) that stabilizes it (Schoenberg and Maquat, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Barreau et al., 2005 and Schoenberg and Maquat, 2012.

claim: ELAVL1 (HuR) is an ARE-binding protein that stabilizes mRNA.
source: Many ARE-binding proteins have been characterized to date that are involved in stability regulation of ARE-hosting mRNAs (Barreau et al., 2005), including Tristetrapolin (TTP), Butyrate Response Factor 1 (BRF1), Heterogeneous Nuclear Ribonucleoprotein (hnRNP) D (also known as AU-Rich Element-Binding Protein 1, AUF1), and KH-type splicing regulatory protein (KSRP), all of which destabilize mRNA, unlike ELAV Like RNA Binding Protein 1 (ELAVL1, also known as HuR) that stabilizes it (Schoenberg and Maquat, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Schoenberg and Maquat, 2012.

claim: RG4s are enriched in UTRs where they regulate many post-transcriptional regulatory processes, including RNA stability.
source: RG4s are enriched in UTRs where they regulate many post-transcriptional regulatory processes, including RNA stability (Dumas et al., 2021), although the detailed mechanisms remain to be elucidated.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dumas et al., 2021.

claim: Upstream open reading frames (uORF) in 5' UTRs can facilitate RNA decay in a translation-dependent manner.
source: For instance, upstream open reading frames (uORF) in 5' UTRs can facilitate RNA decay in a translation-dependent manner, and RG4s in 5' UTRs reduce RNA stability in a ribosome-independent manner (Jia et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jia et al., 2020.

claim: RG4s in 5' UTRs reduce RNA stability in a ribosome-independent manner.
source: For instance, upstream open reading frames (uORF) in 5' UTRs can facilitate RNA decay in a translation-dependent manner, and RG4s in 5' UTRs reduce RNA stability in a ribosome-independent manner (Jia et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jia et al., 2020.

claim: Coding region length and ribosome occupancy are key determinants of RNA stability.
source: For instance, studies examining cellular RNA degradation alongside transcriptional inhibition have shown that coding region length and ribosome occupancy are key determinants of RNA stability (Neymotin et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Neymotin et al., 2015.

claim: Splice junction density is a major factor promoting RNA stability.
source: Additionally, RNA stability inferred from steady-state RNA concentrations normalized against transcription rates has indicated that splice junction density is a major factor promoting RNA stability (Agarwal and Kelley, 2022; Blumberg et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Agarwal and Kelley, 2022 and Blumberg et al., 2021.

claim: A single nucleotide substitution at the 36th position in the 5' UTR of TGFβ3 or its 1723rd 3' UTR position is associated with arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy.
source: For example, a single nucleotide substitution of the 36th position in the 5' UTR of transforming growth factor-β3 (TGFβ3; OMIM# 190230) or its 1723th 3' UTR position is associated with arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (Beffagna et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Beffagna et al., 2005.

claim: Point mutation of the GFPT1 3' UTR results in congenital myasthenic syndrome.
source: Similarly, point mutation of the GFPT1 3' UTR results in congenital myasthenic syndrome.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by the context of the surrounding discussion about UTR mutations and disease.

claim: Mutation of the GFPT1 3' UTR results in a 90% reduction in protein production, potentially due to gain of a miRNA binding site.
source: GFPT1 (Glutamine-Fructose-6-Phosphate Transaminase 1) is the rate-limiting enzyme for hexosamine biosynthesis, and mutation of its 3' UTR results in a 90% reduction in protein production, potentially due to gain of a miRNA binding site (Dusl et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dusl et al., 2015.

claim: The study designed 6555 pairs of 155-nt UTR fragments centering on variants collected from the HGMD and ClinVar disease databases.
source: Therefore, we designed 6555 pairs of 155-nt UTR fragments centering on the variant collected from the HGMD and ClinVar disease databases, and performed time-course assays to examine the relative stability.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the experimental design.

claim: UTR fragments were fused to EGFP coding regions, transcribed in vitro, and transfected into HEK293T or SH-SY5Y cells.
source: First, we fused UTRs to the EGFP coding regions, transcribed them in vitro, and then transfected them into human embryonic kidney cells (HEK293T) or neuroblastoma cells (SH-SY5Y), considering pervasive neurological diseases in the mutation collection.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the experimental procedure.

claim: The relative abundance of reference and mutant alleles was monitored by amplicon sequencing over a time course (30, 75, 120 min for HEK293T; 20, 40, 60 min for SH-SY5Y).
source: Then, we monitored the relative abundance of the reference (ref) and mutant (mt) alleles by amplicon sequencing over a time course (30, 75, 120 min for HEK293T; 20, 40, 60 min for SH-SY5Y) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Variants in both 5' and 3' UTRs significantly altered RNA half-life, with slightly more variants having a negative impact on RNA stability.
source: We observed that variants in both 5' and 3' UTRs significantly altered RNA half-life, with slightly more variants having a negative impact on RNA stability (Figure 1B&C; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Results from three independent experiments are highly consistent, with a Spearman's correlation coefficient >0.93.
source: Our results from three independent experiments are highly consistent, with a Spearman's correlation coefficient >0.93 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: From among 3,700 pairs of valid comparisons, 40 (1.1%) variants displayed significantly altered stability in HEK293T cells.
source: From among 3,700 pairs of valid comparisons, 40 (1.1%) and 839 (22.8%) variants displayed significantly altered stability compared to their ref counterparts in HEK293T and SH-SY5Y cells, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: From among 3,700 pairs of valid comparisons, 839 (22.8%) variants displayed significantly altered stability in SH-SY5Y cells.
source: From among 3,700 pairs of valid comparisons, 40 (1.1%) and 839 (22.8%) variants displayed significantly altered stability compared to their ref counterparts in HEK293T and SH-SY5Y cells, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The regulatory impact of UTR variants on RNA stability was strikingly divergent between HEK293T and SH-SY5Y cell lines.
source: Thus, we observed a significant effect of UTR variation on RNA stability, but their regulatory impact was strikingly divergent between the two tested cell lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: AREs in either the 5' or 3' UTRs generally destabilized RNA.
source: We observed that AREs in either the 5' or 3' UTRs generally destabilized RNA (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: AUUUA/AUUA-containing AREs are associated with RNA destabilization when present in either UTR type.
source: More specifically, AUUUA/AUUA-containing AREs are associated with RNA destabilization when present in either UTR type, whereas in SH-SY5Y cells, extremely U-dominant AREs (U8-10A1-2) stabilized it (Figure 2B), similar to the stabilizing effect of U-stretches described for zebrafish (Rabani et al., 2017; Vejnar et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2B, with additional citation support.

claim: In SH-SY5Y cells, extremely U-dominant AREs (U8-10A1-2) stabilized RNA.
source: More specifically, AUUUA/AUUA-containing AREs are associated with RNA destabilization when present in either UTR type, whereas in SH-SY5Y cells, extremely U-dominant AREs (U8-10A1-2) stabilized it (Figure 2B), similar to the stabilizing effect of U-stretches described for zebrafish (Rabani et al., 2017; Vejnar et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2B, with additional citation support.

claim: GU-rich sequences in 5' UTRs stabilized RNAs in both HEK293T and SH-SY5Y cell lines.
source: In both of the cell lines we tested, GU-rich sequences in 5' UTRs stabilized RNAs (Figure 3B and D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3B and D.

claim: CA- and UG-repeat sequences in 3' UTRs proved the most destabilizing factors in HEK293T cells.
source: In contrast, CA- and UG-repeat sequences—potential binding sites for Insulin Like Growth Factor 2 mRNA Binding Protein 3 (IGF2BP3) and CUGBP Elav-Like Family Member 1 (CELF1)—in 3' UTRs proved the most destabilizing factors in HEK293T cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: UA dinucleotides and other UA-rich sequences are strongly destabilizing for both UTRs.
source: Moreover, we noticed that for both UTRs, UA dinucleotides and other UA-rich sequences—such as WWWWWW (W=A/U; a potential binding motif of Peptidylprolyl Isomerase E (PPIE)), AUUUA (a potential binding motif of ELAV Like RNA Binding Protein 1 (ELAVL1)), and UUUAUA (a potential binding motif of hnRNPA1)—are strongly destabilizing (Figure 3B-E and Figure 4A,C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figures 3B-E and Figure 4A,C.

claim: UA dinucleotides in both UTRs overwhelmed other factors in robustly destabilizing RNAs in SH-SY5Y cells.
source: Most prominently, UA dinucleotides in both UTRs overwhelmed other factors in robustly destabilizing RNAs in SH-SY5Y cells (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: UA dinucleotides alone present a negative correlation with RNA stability, with a Pearson's correlation coefficient of –0.287 for 5' UTRs and –0.377 for 3' UTRs.
source: UA dinucleotides alone present a negative correlation with RNA stability, with a Pearson's correlation coefficient of –0.287 for 5' UTRs and –0.377 for 3' UTRs (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4A and C.

claim: There is a clear propensity for 3' UTRs with stability loss to accumulate gain of UA dinucleotide mutations.
source: We found a clear propensity for 3' UTRs with stability loss to accumulate gain of UA dinucleotide mutations, compared to stabilizing or non-significant mutations (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The acquisition of an additional UA dinucleotide resulted in the destabilization of RNAs in a 5' UTR random library.
source: Notably, the acquisition of an additional UA dinucleotide resulted in the destabilization of RNAs (Figure 4F, Left: 0–1 UA dinucleotide; Right: 1–2 UA dinucleotides).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Elevated UA-dinucleotide ratios in both UTRs significantly promote RNA decay in endogenous mRNA.
source: While exon junction density and transcript length have been suggested as major determinants of RNA half-life in vivo (Agarwal and Kelley, 2022; Blumberg et al., 2021), our findings indicate that elevated UA-dinucleotide ratios in both UTRs significantly promote RNA decay (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G, with additional citation context.

claim: UA-dinucleotide ratios in the coding region are inconsequential for RNA stability.
source: This effect is specific, as such ratios in the coding region are inconsequential.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as part of the analysis of UA-dinucleotide effects.

claim: Library RNAs in SH-SY5Y cells degraded much faster than those in HEK293T cells.
source: Despite undergoing exactly the same procedure, library RNAs in SH-SY5Y cells degraded much faster than those in HEK293T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Ref UTRs whose mutant counterparts significantly destabilized or stabilized RNAs have significantly longer or shorter RNA half-life, respectively.
source: Moreover, for mutant UTRs that significantly destabilized or stabilized RNAs, we found that their ref counterparts are with significantly longer or shorter RNA half-life, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Ref UTRs whose mutant counterparts significantly altered RNA stability tended to harbor more NOVA1 and PPIE binding sites, but fewer FMR1 binding sites.
source: A motif analysis revealed that ref UTRs whose mutant counterparts significantly altered RNA stability tended to harbor more NOVA1 (NOVA Alternative Splicing Regulator 1) and PPIE binding sites, but fewer FMR1 (fragile X mental retardation 1) binding sites (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: UA dinucleotides exhibited a stronger association with RNA half-life than GC content.
source: For both 5' UTRs and 3' UTRs, we observed that UA dinucleotides exhibited a stronger association (i.e. smaller p values) with RNA half-life than GC content.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text based on statistical analysis.

claim: The link between GC content and RNA half-life became non-significant when accounting for UA dinucleotides.
source: Indeed, the link between GC content and RNA half-life became non-significant when we also accounted for UA dinucleotides (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The interaction term (UA-diNT% × GC%) proved significant for three out of four experimental groups.
source: Moreover, the interaction term (UA-diNT% × GC%) proved significant for three out of four experimental groups (SH-SY5Y 5' UTR: p = 0.18, 3' UTR: p = 0.00047, HEK293T 5' UTR: p = 0.0062, 3' UTR: p = 1.2e-7), supporting that GC content influences the effect of UA dinucleotides.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text with specific p-values from statistical analysis.

claim: UA dinucleotides strongly destabilized RNA in the context of low GC content (bottom 50%), but their effects were neutralized somewhat under scenarios of high GC content (top 50%).
source: We found that UA dinucleotides strongly destabilized RNA in the context of low GC content (bottom 50%), but their effects were neutralized somewhat under scenarios of high GC content (top 50%; Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The protective effect of GC content was remarkably strong for high UA-dinucleotide ratios but was barely detectable for low UA-dinucleotide ratios.
source: Conversely, the protective effect of GC content was remarkably strong for high UA-dinucleotide ratios but was barely detectable for low UA-dinucleotide ratios (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The stabilizing or destabilizing effects of UA deletion or addition, respectively, were only observed for low GC content.
source: Moreover, the stabilizing or destabilizing effects of UA deletion or addition, respectively, were only observed for low GC content, further supporting that high GC content hinders the destabilizing effect of UA dinucleotides (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: UA dinucleotides are enriched in P-body-resident mRNAs.
source: We uncovered a positive correlation between UA dinucleotides and RNA P-body localization, especially for those occurring in 3' UTRs (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: A greater UA dinucleotide-stabilizing effect in P-bodies was observed when GC content is low.
source: For both UTR types, we observed a greater UA dinucleotide-stabilizing effect in P-bodies when GC content is low (Figure 5D), consistent with our MPRA dataset.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The RNA group with multiple RBP binding partners per UA dinucleotide displayed longer half-life compared to the group with few binding partners.
source: In doing so, we revealed that the RNA group with multiple binding partners indeed displayed longer half-life compared to the group with few binding partners.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text based on analysis of RBP binding data.

claim: Half-life obtained by actinomycin D treatment were highly correlated with the MPRA result (ρ=0.8).
source: Half-life obtained by the actinomycin D treatment were highly correlated with the MPRA result (ρ=0.8) in accordance with numbers of RBP binding sites per UA dinucleotide.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text with a specific correlation coefficient.

claim: UA-binding RBPs play roles in either safeguarding or promoting RNA degradation.
source: By correlating the binding of UA dinucleotide-binding proteins with RNA half-life, we identified UA-binding RBPs that play roles in either safeguarding or promoting RNA degradation (Figure 5J; Figure 5—figure supplement 2E; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5J and Figure 5—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The 5' UTRs of genes responsible for regulating appetite, apoptosis and synaptic signaling display the highest UA-dinucleotide ratios.
source: We found that the 5' UTRs of genes responsible for regulating appetite, apoptosis and synaptic signaling display the highest UA-dinucleotide ratios and those involved in glutathione metabolism exhibit the lowest (Figure 6A; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Genes linked to integrin activation, the interleukin-mediated pathway and B-cell differentiation have the highest UA-dinucleotide ratios in 3' UTRs.
source: In terms of 3' UTRs, genes linked to integrin activation, the interleukin-mediated pathway and B-cell differentiation have the highest UA-dinucleotide ratios (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The gene groups with high UA-dinucleotide ratios in both UTRs are all related to the immune response.
source: Notably, the gene groups in the first quadrant, reflecting UA-dinucleotide ratios in both UTRs being above background levels, are all related to the immune response.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text based on analysis of gene groups.

claim: Two 3' UTR mutations that resulted in aberrant expression of both RNA and proteins (DDP4 and CASP7) were A/T deletions in TA-rich sequences with increased RNA and protein expression levels.
source: Interestingly, two 3' UTR mutations that resulted in aberrant expression of both RNA and proteins (DDP4 [Dipeptidyl Peptidase 4] and CASP7 [Caspase 7], respectively) were A/T deletions in TA-rich sequences with increased RNA and protein expression levels (Figure 7A and B), in agreement with our findings that UA-rich sequences are the most influential stability determinants (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: P values were skewed towards the stability-altering variants, indicating that TWB subjects harboring stability-altering UTR variants are more likely to display abnormal biochemical phenotypes.
source: We observed that p values were skewed towards the stability-altering variants, indicating that TWB subjects harboring stability-altering UTR variants are more likely to display abnormal biochemical phenotypes.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text based on analysis of Taiwan Biobank data.

claim: APOC3 is involved in metabolizing triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, and its mutation has been associated with low plasma triglyceride levels.
source: APOC3 is involved in metabolizing triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, and its mutation has been associated with low plasma triglyceride levels (Borén et al., 2020; Goyal et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Borén et al., 2020 and Goyal et al., 2021.

claim: The UA-dinucleotide ratio rather than GC content or folding energy explained RNA stability data better.
source: The UA-dinucleotide ratio rather than GC content or folding energy explained our RNA stability data better, implying that specific sequence recognition by trans factors and not simply regulation according to structuredness is the underlying control mechanism.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text based on analysis of the data.

claim: RNase A cleaves 3'–5' phosphodiester bonds with a specificity for pyrimidines (U/C) at the main anchoring site and purines (A/G) at the secondary site.
source: RNase A cleaves 3'–5' phosphodiester bonds with a specificity for pyrimidines (U/C) at the main anchoring site and purines (A/G) at the secondary site (Sorrentino, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sorrentino, 2010.

claim: Kinetic analysis has revealed a >100-fold preference for UpA than UpG substrates for the human RNase A family (RNase 1–7).
source: Kinetic analysis has revealed a >100-fold preference for UpA than UpG substrates for the human RNase A family (RNase 1–7, RNase 8 was not studied in this report) (Prats-Ejarque et al., 2019), consistent with our finding that UA dinucleotides represent the most destabilizing sequence motifs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Prats-Ejarque et al., 2019.

claim: Transcript and UTR length is negatively correlated with RNA stability.
source: It was reported that transcript and UTR length is negatively correlated with RNA stability (Neymotin et al., 2015; Blumberg et al., 2021), implying that increased RNA mass could be susceptible to endonuclease attack.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Neymotin et al., 2015 and Blumberg et al., 2021.

claim: More 5' UTR variants than those in 3' UTRs caused stability changes.
source: Our MPRA data revealed that more 5' UTR variants than those in 3' UTRs caused stability changes (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Stability-altering variants of both UTR types are associated with skewed biomarker or disease accessions in the TWB.
source: Moreover, we found that stability-altering variants of both UTR types are associated with skewed biomarker or disease accessions in the TWB.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text based on analysis of Taiwan Biobank data.

claim: Mutational gain of UA dinucleotides is linked to diminished RNA half-life.
source: At the sequence level, our results indicate that mutational gain of UA dinucleotides is linked to diminished RNA half-life (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4E.
